entities.name: Ulm Minster
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Ulm Minster (Ulmer Münster), a Lutheran Gothic church in Ulm, Baden-Württemberg begun in 1377 and whose main spire was completed in 1890 (after 513 years of construction), holds the world's tallest church steeple at 161.53 meters — surpassing Cologne Cathedral's 157.38 meters to claim the title that the medieval builders had planned but could not achieve. The minster is a civic church (never a cathedral — Ulm had no bishop), built and funded by the city's burghers as a statement of urban pride and civic wealth.

The foundation stone was laid in 1377 at the decision of Ulm's town council — a civic rather than episcopal institution — to build the grandest church possible as a statement of Ulm's commercial prosperity. The initial architect Ulrich von Ensingen developed the design, with successive master builders refining the drawings over centuries. When the Reformation reached Ulm in 1530, the city converted to Lutheranism and the church became a Protestant minster, abandoning Catholic liturgical requirements while continuing physical construction.

The 19th-century completion was motivated by German nationalist romanticism — completing medieval projects became a statement of German cultural identity (Cologne Cathedral completed 1880, Ulm 1890). The minster's 768-step spiral staircase to the tower platform, and the 15th-century choir stalls (154 misericords), represent the building's great interior treasures. The city of Ulm was 80% destroyed in a single RAF bombing raid on December 17, 1944, but the minster survived intact — its steeple visible above the rubble — a symbol of continuity amid destruction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ulm Minster's 513-year construction — from 1377 to 1890 — producing the world's tallest church spire is the most ambitious multi-generational civic construction project in history, and its survival amid Ulm's 80% wartime destruction made it a symbol of German cultural continuity.
